title: Forgetting to Improve: Principled Data Removal in Active Learning
claim: A standard model lets detrimental data distort predictions in the target region; selectively removing that data gives tighter, more accurate predictions.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, shared axes, left baseline vs right ours, arrow annotations
description: Two side-by-side 1-D regression plots share the same axes: x from -0.2 to 1.0 and f(x) from -8 to 2. The left panel is titled 'Homoscedastic GP' and the right panel 'Forgetting to Improve'. Each panel shows a grey ground-truth curve f* with a sharp downward spike near x=0.15, purple sample dots, a blue GP mean curve and a teal uncertainty band. A pale green vertical strip marks the target region A. On the left, the band is wide across A, and black curved arrows labelled 'Detrimental data points' point at the spike samples. On the right, the spike samples are removed and the band is tight around the mean. Arrows labelled 'Contributing points outside of target region' point at the remaining samples. A legend on the far right lists A, f*, Samples, mu_GP and sigma_GP.
caption: Influence of detrimental data structures based on the Dow Jones data set [4]. (Left) Homoscedastic GP absorbs detrimental structures in the noise, resulting in uncertain predictions in A. (Right) Forgetting to Improve (F2I) removes detrimental data to improve predictions in A.
abstract: The uncertainty of a statistical model is most commonly factorized into an aleatoric and an epistemic part. This factorization changes how predictions are interpreted in downstream decision tasks. Importantly, except for the idealistic scenario with no model mismatch, the quantification is a characteristic of the model and not the data generating process. In this paper, we propose Forgetting to Improve a method that reduces this discrepancy by incorporating the task into the modeling framework. Our key insight is to acknowledge that in scenarios of model mismatch, data can have a detrimental effect on the modeling for a specific task. Based on this insight, we propose an influence function for Gaussian process models that allows for principled removal of detrimental data samples. We showcase the flexibility of this approach by demonstrating significant improvements across a range of tasks, including Bayesian optimization, model-based reinforcement learning, and transductive learning.
